planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded, humid hanging basket in bright, indirect light in a loose, well-drained, chunky epiphytic mix; strap-leaf anthurium is best displayed hanging so its long pendulous leaves can drape freely.

directions: Grow as a houseplant or shaded, humid hanging basket in bright, indirect light in a loose, well-drained, chunky epiphytic mix; strap-leaf anthurium is best displayed hanging so its long pendulous leaves can drape freely. Extraordinarily long, narrow, ribbon-like leaves dangle several feet down from a short central stem, an unusual pendulous growth form completely unlike the broad heart-shaped leaves of florist anthuriums, with slender, string-like fruit spikes that dangle even further once the plant flowers and sets seed. Native to Ecuadorian and Colombian cloud forests, where it grows as an epiphyte high in the tree canopy, it is best mounted or grown in a hanging basket where its dramatic trailing foliage can be fully appreciated rather than confined to an upright pot. Water when the mix approaches dryness, maintain high humidity, and provide bright, filtered light for the longest, healthiest leaves.

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded, humid hanging basket in bright, indirect light in a loose, well-drained, chunky epiphytic mix; Wendlinger's anthurium is best displayed hanging so its long pendulous leaves can drape freely.

directions: Grow as a houseplant or shaded, humid hanging basket in bright, indirect light in a loose, well-drained, chunky epiphytic mix; Wendlinger's anthurium is best displayed hanging so its long pendulous leaves can drape freely. Long, glossy, strap-shaped leaves with a distinctly quilted, corrugated surface texture hang gracefully downward, similar in overall form to the related strap-leaf anthurium but with broader, more heavily textured foliage and a more pronounced pleated pattern along each leaf. Native to Costa Rican and Panamanian cloud forests, it grows epiphytically in the wild and is best replicated in cultivation with a hanging basket or mounted display that allows its pendulous leaves to hang free rather than a standard upright pot. Water when the mix approaches dryness, maintain high humidity, and provide bright, filtered light for the best leaf texture and length.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container stock after last frost in rich, moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Black Magic alocasia is frost-tender and best grown as a container specimen moved indoors for winter outside zones 10-11.

directions: Plant divisions or container stock after last frost in rich, moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Black Magic alocasia is frost-tender and best grown as a container specimen moved indoors for winter outside zones 10-11. Small, narrow, deeply lobed leaves emerge an almost pure black-purple with a subtle metallic sheen, among the darkest foliage of any commonly grown alocasia, held on slender stems that keep the compact plant well below a foot tall even at maturity. Native to Sumatra, it is prized by collectors for its intensely dark, dramatic coloring, working well as a small accent among lighter-leaved companions in a shaded tropical container grouping. Provide consistent warmth and high humidity, protect from direct sun which can bleach the dark pigment, and allow the potting mix to dry slightly between waterings to avoid rot at the tuber.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container stock after last frost in rich, moist, well-drained soil in partial shade; Portei alocasia grows into a large, tree-like specimen and needs substantial room and a large container to reach its full size.

directions: Plant divisions or container stock after last frost in rich, moist, well-drained soil in partial shade; Portei alocasia grows into a large, tree-like specimen and needs substantial room and a large container to reach its full size. Deeply and dramatically lobed, arrow-shaped leaves with pronounced finger-like divisions are carried atop a thick, upright, trunk-like stem that can eventually reach well over head height, giving this species a bold, tree-fern-like architectural presence unlike the smaller clumping alocasias more commonly grown as houseplants. Native to the Philippines, it is one of the larger-growing alocasia species available to home growers, best suited to a spacious sunroom, greenhouse, or sheltered tropical patio where its eventual size can be accommodated. Provide consistent warmth, high humidity, and bright indirect light, and expect the trunk to elongate and the plant to take on a more architectural form as it matures over several years.

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant trained onto a moss pole or bark slab in bright, indirect light in well-drained, chunky, humus-rich potting mix; Korthals' shingle vine presses its juvenile leaves flat against a climbing support and needs that vertical surface to grow well.

directions: Grow as a houseplant trained onto a moss pole or bark slab in bright, indirect light in well-drained, chunky, humus-rich potting mix; Korthals' shingle vine presses its juvenile leaves flat against a climbing support and needs that vertical surface to grow well. In its juvenile climbing stage, small, glossy, overlapping leaves press tightly flat against tree bark or a moss pole in a dense, shingled pattern, a distinctive growth habit shared with a handful of other aroid vines and prized by collectors for the tidy, textured wall of foliage it creates. As the vine matures and reaches better light, its leaves grow progressively larger and eventually become perforated, similar in appearance to a small monstera, once it is well established and climbing vigorously. Provide a broad, moist support such as a sphagnum-covered pole for the aerial roots to grip, mist regularly to keep humidity high, and be patient, since the shift from small shingling leaves to larger mature foliage can take considerable time.
sources: American Society for Horticultural Science reference

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded hanging basket in bright, indirect light in well-drained, chunky potting mix; Manta Ray scindapsus climbs readily on a moss pole and develops larger, more richly marked leaves with vertical support.

directions: Grow as a houseplant or shaded hanging basket in bright, indirect light in well-drained, chunky potting mix; Manta Ray scindapsus climbs readily on a moss pole and develops larger, more richly marked leaves with vertical support. Thick, glossy, deep green leaves are marbled with irregular silver and gray patches and carried on distinctively winged, ridged petioles that give the plant a bold, slightly rugged texture compared to the smoother satin pothos more commonly sold. Native to Southeast Asian forests, it grows more vigorously and with larger foliage than many Scindapsus pictus cultivars once given a support to climb, making it a striking specimen for a moss pole in a bright room. Let the potting mix dry between waterings, provide bright indirect light for the strongest silver marbling, and mist occasionally to keep the thick leaves dust-free.
sources: American Society for Horticultural Science reference

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container on a moss pole in bright, indirect light in well-drained, chunky, humus-rich potting mix; White Wizard philodendron needs strong indirect light to sustain its white variegation and resents cold, drafty conditions.

directions: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container on a moss pole in bright, indirect light in well-drained, chunky, humus-rich potting mix; White Wizard philodendron needs strong indirect light to sustain its white variegation and resents cold, drafty conditions. Broad, dark green leaves are irregularly marked with bold patches and speckles of creamy white variegation on pale green petioles, closely resembling the similar 'White Knight' and 'White Princess' philodendrons but with somewhat lighter stem coloring, a distinction collectors watch for when identifying which particular white-variegated philodendron they have. As a climbing aroid it develops larger, more heavily variegated leaves when trained up a moss pole rather than left to trail, growing steadily under good light and warmth. Provide strong indirect light to maintain the white variegation, remove any fully white (chlorophyll-free) growth that will eventually decline, and keep humidity moderate to high.
sources: American Society for Horticultural Science reference

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container in bright, indirect light in well-drained, chunky, humus-rich potting mix; Ring of Fire philodendron is a compact, self-heading (non-climbing) selection that needs no moss pole or trellis.

directions: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container in bright, indirect light in well-drained, chunky, humus-rich potting mix; Ring of Fire philodendron is a compact, self-heading (non-climbing) selection that needs no moss pole or trellis. Deeply serrated, oak-leaf-shaped foliage emerges heavily speckled and streaked in shades of cream, yellow, orange, and pink over a green base, with each leaf displaying a unique, unpredictable mix of colors and patterns that shift as it matures, giving the plant an almost painterly, ever-changing appearance. Its compact, non-vining rosette habit and deeply cut leaf margins set it apart texturally from smoother, rounder-leaved philodendrons, and the unpredictable color patterning makes each individual plant unique. Provide bright indirect light to maintain the vivid multicolor variegation, water when the top inch of potting mix dries, and rotate the pot occasionally for even growth.
sources: American Society for Horticultural Science reference
